name: Caesarism
scope: Caesarism as the scholarship defines it (Prutsch 2020, Casper): the modern concept coined and given its polemical meaning by Romieu's 1850 L'ère des Césars, and developed by Weber (plebiscitary mass democracy led by a charismatic leader), Spengler (Cäsarismus as the closing phase of a civilization) and Gramsci (Caesarism as an arbiter's solution to a catastrophic equilibrium of social forces, progressive or reactionary). The practical cases the sources discuss are Napoleon I, Napoleon III and Bismarck. Excludes Bonapartism, which has its own entry, and the ecclesiastical sense of the word (Heard's 1877 'Caesarism and clericalism' uses it for state control of the Church, a different thing). Excludes the loose modern use of the word for any populist strongman, which the sources do not define.

summary: Caesarism is personal, plebiscitary rule in which one commanding figure, claiming to stand above warring classes and parties, resolves a crisis that ordinary politics cannot. In Gramsci's account it arises when opposed forces balance each other catastrophically and a great personality arbitrates; in Weber's it means plebiscitary elections, disdain for parliament and no autonomous powers within government. Gramsci distinguishes progressive from reactionary Caesarism.
